summary: Source Description (SDES) items are normally sent in RTCP, but sometimes they need to arrive faster, for example when a new source joins an RTP session and receivers need to know who it is. This proposed standard defines an RTP header extension that carries SDES items in the media packets themselves, speeding up delivery.

eli5.summary: When a new person joins a video call, others want to know who it is straight away. Instead of waiting for a slow announcement, the name tag is attached directly to the first things they send.

subtitle: Carry RTCP source description items such as CNAME inside RTP media packets so receivers get them sooner.

tldr.problem: Source Description (SDES) items such as CNAME normally travel in RTCP, which can be slow to arrive when a new source joins an RTP session. Receivers may be unable to relate or synchronize the new stream until they have it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an RTP header extension, using the general mechanism of RFC 5285, that carries an SDES item as UTF-8 text in the one-byte or two-byte format. It also sets a URN subspace for these items and registers CNAME.
tldr.outcome: SDES items can arrive together with the first media packets. Only items that need timely delivery should use it, and security and privacy need care because the items can be sensitive. The RFC has been updated by RFC 8843 and RFC 9143.

today: RFC 7941 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8843 and RFC 9143, so read those alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Source Description (SDES) items are normally carried in their own RTCP packet type. RFC 7941 defines an RTP header extension that can carry selected SDES items instead, which speeds up working out the relationship and synchronization context of a new stream (SSRC) in an RTP session. It complements RTCP delivery; it does not replace it.

Not every SDES item belongs here. Some items bind streams or identify synchronization contexts and have strict timeliness needs, while many others do not. Privacy matters too: the Name and Location items are highly sensitive and should not be sent without strong security, and no use case needs them when the first RTP packets arrive. So only appropriate items, such as CNAME, are registered for the header extension.
sections.eli5: Some facts about a sender are needed at once, like their name tag. Others can wait. Only the ones needed at once go on the fast lane.

sections.title: Why Faster Delivery Helps
sections.content:
SDES items describe one SSRC. The CNAME is commonly needed when the first RTP packet for an SSRC arrives, or at least before the first media can be played out. Without it the synchronization context cannot be determined, so related streams cannot be correctly synchronized.

New SSRCs appear mostly when media sources are added, either because an endpoint adds a source or because more participants join a multi-party session. A new SSRC can also appear after an SSRC collision, which forces both colliding parties to pick new ones.

The RFC links this to RFC 6051, which defines a header extension for rapid synchronization carrying the clock information from RTCP sender reports. That extension assumes the CNAME binding is already known, which signaling can provide in some cases but not all. Carrying CNAME in a header extension closes the gap. The RFC also notes that a media description identifier (MID), matching the SDP a=mid attribute, could benefit from timely delivery, and its header extension is defined in the SDP bundling work.
sections.eli5: To line up sound and picture from a new person, you need to know who they are. Waiting for a slow announcement leaves you guessing.

sections.title: The Header Extension Formats
sections.content:
The extension builds on the general RTP header extension mechanism of RFC 5285, which defines a short (one-byte) and a long (two-byte) element header. The ID field identifies both the extension and the SDES item type. The mapping is agreed in signaling using a URN registered for each suitable SDES item.

In the one-byte format, a 4-bit ID is followed by a 4-bit len, and the data is len+1 bytes of UTF-8 text, so 1 to 16 bytes. In the two-byte format, an 8-bit ID is followed by an 8-bit len, and the data is len bytes of UTF-8 text, so 0 to 255 bytes. Either way any SDES item fits.

The one-byte form SHOULD be used when all other header extensions support it and every SDES text value is at most 16 bytes. RFC 5285 does not allow mixing the two forms for one SSRC, so if any SDES item needs the two-byte form, all other extensions MUST use it too. As an example, a CNAME built per RFC 7022 from a 96-bit random value before base64 encoding fits the one-byte form.
sections.eli5: There are a small envelope and a bigger envelope. Pick the small one if everything fits, but everything in the same stream must use the same size.

sections.title: Using It in Practice
sections.content:
Packet size. Extra header bytes grow each packet. Sending CNAME, a MID and the RFC 6051 rapid sync extension together is likely to take at least 16+3+8 bytes of data plus 7 bytes of one-byte headers and two bytes of padding to align to 32 bits, 36 bytes in total. If a payload was sized to the MTU without allowing for this, the packet can be fragmented at the IP level, which hurts loss rates. Encoders and packetizers should cope with varying payload limits, or assume a reasonable worst case.

When to send. The general advice is to send the extension only when needed, since RTCP repeats SDES items all session long. How many repeats are needed depends on packet loss: N repetitions reach a delivery probability of 1-P^N, where P is the loss probability. Items need not go in every packet of a set that shares fate, such as one video frame. For small groups, RTCP feedback such as the XR Loss RLE report block or generic NACK can show when to stop or repeat.

Use cases. For a new SSRC, aim for high delivery probability to everyone. For a late joiner, send to the newcomers only, for instance when RTCP from them or a Rapid Resynchronization Request triggers it. When SDES information changes and is tied to the media, the header extension beats RTCP because the update arrives with the related media.

Versus RTCP. With an AVPF-based profile an extra RTCP packet can be sent early, but it is a separate packet with no fate sharing with the media, and RTCP has no sequence numbers or feedback on itself, so delivery is hard to confirm.
sections.eli5: Stick the name tag on the first few packets, enough times that at least one makes it, but not on every packet or you waste room.

sections.title: Avoiding Update Flaps
sections.content:
An SDES item can arrive both in RTP header extensions and in RTCP, so a value may flap back and forth when it changes. One cause is reordering, where an old packet arrives after one with the new value. The other is different code paths: an RTCP packet built before the update may sit in a buffer while RTP packets already carry the new value.

Receivers can avoid most of this. SDES items in RTP packets with the same or a lower extended sequence number than the last change MUST NOT be applied. For RTCP, the sender report timestamp gives the approximate send time, and an SDES item in an RTCP packet that is older than the last RTP packet carrying the item can be ignored. The RFC warns that pacing can make timestamps differ from actual send time.

On header compression, the extension data is not part of what ROHC compresses, but the X bit is classed as rarely changing, which may lower compression efficiency when extensions are used often.
sections.eli5: If an old name tag shows up late, ignore it and keep the newest one.

sections.title: Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the base URN urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes and created a sub-registry, "RTP SDES Compact Header Extensions", for URNs starting with urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes:. Registration follows Expert Review with extra requirements. The item MUST also be registered in the "RTP SDES item types" registry, security and privacy considerations MUST be given, and the registration MUST explain why timely delivery justifies a header extension rather than RTCP only.

The initial entry is urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes:cname for the CNAME item.
sections.eli5: There is now an official list of which name-tag items may use the fast lane. Right now only CNAME is on it, and new ones must explain why they need it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
SDES items can be sensitive. CNAME, NAME, EMAIL, PHONE, LOC and H323-CADDR may be private, NOTE and PRIV may hold sensitive data, and TOOL can help profile implementations. A short-term random CNAME has minimal impact, a user@host CNAME raises privacy concerns, and one made from a MAC address allows long-term tracking.

Where RTCP has confidentiality protection, the SDES header extensions MUST be protected too. For SRTP users that means encrypted header extensions per RFC 6904, with commensurate algorithm strength, and SHOULD use the same primitives as for the matching RTCP items. SRTP only protects the next trusted RTP/RTCP hop, not necessarily end to end.

A received item could cause heavy processing, storage or traffic, though CNAME is only a minor risk. Because items establish relationships between streams, there SHOULD be strong integrity protection and source authentication, or an attacker could create wrong bindings.
sections.eli5: A name tag can give away private facts. Lock it up the same way you lock the slow-lane version, and make sure nobody can swap it.

fields.name: ID
fields.desc: Identifies the SDES item type, as mapped in signaling.

fields.name: len
fields.desc: Number of data bytes is len+1.

fields.name: SDES item text value
fields.desc: UTF-8 text; 1 to 16 bytes in total.
